newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Taleban acting defence minister wounded in battle.
newsitem.headline: Taleban acting defence minister wounded in battle.

text.p: The acting defence minister of the Islamic Taleban administration in Kabul was wounded in fighting with former government forces in the Salang area north of the capital, Taleban sources said on Tuesday.
The sources said Mullah Abdul Razzak, a member of the Taleban's ruling six-man interim shura (council) set up after the Islamic radicals seized Kabul, was not critically wounded.
"He is a little wounded. He is okay, no danger," one Taleban source said.
The sources said another Taleban commander, Mohammad Agha, had been wounded in recent fighting with forces commanded by ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
They did not say exactly when the two men had been wounded, or give any details of their injuries.
Taleban sources said on Monday that a senior Taleban commander, Mullah Abdul Ahad, had been killed in fighting.
Taleban fighters have been strengthening their defences around Kabul after weekend battles in which Masood drove the Islamic militia most of the way back to the capital.
The fundamentalist Taleban, rulers of most of Afghanistan for the past two weeks, on Monday admitted losing towns on the road north of Kabul but vowed they would recapture them.

The Taleban captured Kabul on September 27 and pushed north to besiege Masood's forces in his Panjsher Valley stronghold, but had made little headway when one of Masood's commanders launched a devastating counter-attack in the nearby Salang Pass, isolating a Taleban force and inflicting heavy casualties.
More than 200 Taleban wounded had been ferried to the southern city of Kandahar in the past few days, Taleban sources said.
About 150 wounded men had been admitted on Sunday to the city's Mirwais hospital, run by the International Committee of the Red Cross, and 70 more had arrived on Monday.
Other wounded Taleban fighters had been admitted to a German hospital in Kandahar and about 70 had been brought to the Pakistani border city of Quetta, the sources said.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press quoted witnesses in the eastern Afghanistan city of Jalalabad on Monday as saying that many Taleban casualties had been taken to hospital there.
"We have seen lots of wounded and there are not enough beds for them, so they are lying in the corridors," one witness said.
A Taleban spokesman in Quetta, Mullah Juma Khan Akhund, said many volunteers were leaving Kandahar, base of the movement's reclusive leader Mullah Mohammad Omar, for the front.
"Hundreds are leaving daily," Akhund said. "It is a jihad (holy war). People come voluntarily to join it."
